papers.title: Structural latent dimension: deterministic geometry and local Fisher structure
papers.abstract: We study the \emph{structural dimension} of a second-order object: the minimum latent dimension that remains necessary relative to a declared class of competing dependence. Building on minimum-rank factor analysis and low-rank-plus-sparse decomposition, we use distances to lower-dimensional classes to describe inference near structural ambiguity. General distance and tangent-cone facts yield confidence statements and local margins. For rank-zero competitors with bounded residual degree, we derive exact maximum-weight $b$-matching formulas, support-slack tangent cones and sparse-spike angles; a shared residual support across a field can produce separation absent pointwise. We give positive-semidefinite brackets, a dimension-free Gaussian likelihood expansion, an exact quotient by the tangent of a low-rank background, and a detection floor from the margin. Equal-angle configurations with different branch multiplicities motivate static and spectral detection conjectures. Joint low-rank/residual profiling and the sharp composite information boundaries remain open.

papers.title: Anomaly detection using surprisals
papers.abstract: Anomaly detection methods are widely used but often rely on ad hoc rules or strong assumptions, and they often focus on tail events, missing "inlier" anomalies that occur in low-density gaps between modes. We propose a unified framework that defines an anomaly as an observation with unusually low probability under a (possibly mis-specified) model. For each observation we compute its surprisal (the negative log generalized density) and define an anomaly score as the probability of a surprisal at least as large as that observed. This reduces anomaly detection for complex univariate or multivariate data to estimating the upper tail of a univariate surprisal distribution. We develop two model-robust approximations to these tail probabilities: an empirical approximation based on the observed surprisal distribution and a GPD approximation that fits a Generalized Pareto Distribution above a high threshold. For the empirical approximation we give conditions under which tail ordering is preserved and derive finite-sample confidence guarantees via the Dvoretzky-Kiefer-Wolfowitz inequality. For the GPD approximation we establish broad tail conditions ensuring classical extreme-value behavior. Simulations and applications to French mortality, Test-cricket and Old Faithful geyser data show the approach remains effective under substantial model mis-specification.
